text: Didn't expect Jensen Huang to serve me hot green tea. (No, the video isn’t AI-generated). NVIDIA treated tech leaders for some Monkey King opera. Jensen showed up, press followed. We spoke about SF, AI, Trump. I asked him about venture capital. But there is more to the story than what he said. Lets' look at why he said it, who was there, and what happened during the opera. Embedded in the subtext is a masterful message no one can ignore. The facts: 1. 🐵 He brought his tech superpower friends to see Monkey King - casual! 2. ❤️ He and Lori donate $5M/year to the SF Opera - lovely! 3. 👯 He underscored the role of the arts in the age of AI - important! 4. 🤖 He said “SF is back!” “An AI City” attracting global talent - evident! 5. 🤔 He was one of two people who rang up Trump urging against sending the National Guard into SF —and Trump listened - baller! 6. 🧧 I asked if NVIDIA is going deeper into VC; he gave three reasons (in the video). And then the subtext: In the theatre. The VIP box seats. There was something else. I couldn’t shake it. As I took my seat, I saw Tier 1 VC partners, big-tech CEOs (Sundar included), and decacorn founders do the same. The way everyone settled in felt like a quiet rehearsal for a larger play. A timeless story about POWER unraveled: The quest for absolute power. How power can subjugate others or uplift them. How power can be granted, given, and shared. But Jensen directed the deeper message: As AI accelerates in power, tech titans secure NVIDIA chips to conjure its use -> Venture capital funds AI applications for the masses -> Government leaders battle to secure intelligence as utility for their citizens. Jensen just sat their butts down for a 2.5 hour lecture in full vibrato and monkey makeup - an instruction manual how to use their power like an enlightened being would. Jensen’s made his message is clear. Those who continue to accumulate power must remember to empower others with it. text: Everyone in tech should take a comedy class. In 2018, I took a comedy class in Seattle, and it completely changed how I approach communication. Here is what comedians taught me about being data-driven: 🎭 1. Test your material in different "environments": Comedians don't just perform once and call it done. They test the same joke across different audiences, venues, and times. If something bombs, they don't take it personally—it could be an outlier. 👀 2. Read the room, not just the words Good comedians watch facial expressions, body language, and energy shifts. They notice which specific words get laughs and what the audience looks like. This isn't just about hearing—it's about seeing the full picture. 🎯 3. Master the three levels of listening(This came from my coach training): - Level 1: I'm just waiting for my turn to talk - Level 2: I'm fully engaged in our conversation - Level 3: I'm aware of the entire environment—the room, the energy, what's happening around us Most of us live in Level 1. But the best communicators—whether they're comedians, coaches, or data scientists—operate at Level 3.They're not just delivering information. They're reading the audience, adapting in real-time, and paying attention to everything that's not being said. What's your favorite unexpected place you've learned communication skills? text: 90% of the time, imposter syndrome hits overachievers, not the underperformers. The people with high standards tend to zoom in on what they don't know instead of what they do. I see this with the data scientists I coach. They're technically brilliant, but tormented by thoughts like "Everyone else seems to know everything" or "I'm the only one who had to Google that." Here's what they don't realize: everyone has knowledge gaps. The solution is not about overcoming imposter syndrome - it's about accepting that you're not perfect and believing you're enough as you are. This is a process, not a quick fix. But here's what helps: connecting with your peers. Share your struggles. Ask how others overcame similar challenges. You'll discover everyone is figuring it out as they go. In my group coaching sessions, people tell me they feel more confident just by hearing others' questions. Sometimes being seen and heard matters more than getting advice. You're not a machine at your company. Talk to your coworkers about things beyond work. When you realize you're not the only one with knowledge gaps, imposter syndrome starts to fade. You stop seeing yourself as the fraud among experts and start seeing yourself as one expert among many. This clip is from my chat with Jiajia Zhou, data scientist at Meta on "Daliana's Game" podcast. I also write a newsletter about communication skills and visibility at work, learn more: https://lnkd.in/euvsPYYR …more

text: Before I quit my full-time job in 2023, I kept telling myself: "Maybe I should wait until it's more stable." However, I discovered a paradox: to stabilize my business, it required more of my time and mental energy. Which meant I had to create more time and headspace for it. The oxymoron became clear - I couldn't build stability while dividing my attention between two demanding priorities. Sometimes short-term instability is the necessary step for long-term stability on your own terms. I've gotten used to the variations that come with running a business. The unpredictable income months. The sudden opportunities. The constant pivoting and adaptation. And I'm glad I took that leap. Not because it's been easy, but because it makes me feel more alive, have more impact, and I get to define my own definition of career success. I want to play Dailana's Game. This clip is from my conversation with my friend Evelyn, who quit Amazon to become a lifestyle vlogger. Search "Daliana's Game" in your favorite podcast platforms to listen/watch it. To be clear, I don't think you have to leave your 9-to-5 job to design your ideal career. It could look different for everyone.
